label: Sixth-edition aphorisms
title: Aphorism § 87
text:
§ 87



 And thus the physician obtains more precise information respecting
          each particular detail, but without ever framing his questions so as to suggest the answer
          to the patient 1 , so that he shall only have to answer yes or no;
          else he will be misled to answer in the affirmative or negative something untrue, half
          true, or not strictly correct, either from indolence or in order to please his
          interrogator, from which a false picture of the disease and an unsuitable mode of
          treatment must result.



1  For instance the physician should not ask, Was not this or
          that circumstance present? He should never be guilty of making such suggestions, which
          tend to seduce the patient into giving a false answer and a false account of his symptoms.
